blocks.title: Diffraction
blocks.text: Diffraction is the bending of light around obstacles and the spreading of light waves into the geometrical shadow of an obstacle.

If the number of slits in an interference experiment is increased while the spacing of neighbouring slits stays the same, the maxima stay in the same positions but become progressively narrower than with two slits. Because these maxima are so narrow, their angular positions, and hence the wavelength, can be measured very precisely.

blocks.title: Diffraction grating
blocks.text: A diffraction grating is an array of a large number of parallel slits, all of the same width and spaced equal distances d between their centres. The spacing d is called the grating spacing; the slits are often called rulings or lines.

The first grating was made by Fraunhofer using fine wires. Gratings can be made by scratching many equally spaced grooves on glass or metal with a diamond point, or by photographic reduction of a pattern of black and white stripes. Fig 15.16 is a cross-section of a transmission grating; the diagram shows only five slits, but an actual grating may have several thousand. A plane monochromatic wave falls normally on the grating. Far-field (Fraunhofer) conditions are assumed: the screen is far enough away that all rays leaving the grating towards one point of the screen can be considered parallel.

The principal maxima occur in the directions for which the path difference between neighbouring slits is a whole number of wavelengths: d sin(theta) = n lambda, where n = 0, +/-1, +/-2, +/-3, ... (15.7). When a grating with hundreds or thousands of slits is lit by parallel monochromatic light, the pattern is a series of very sharp lines (Fig 15.17). The n = +/-1 lines are the first-order lines, n = +/-2 the second-order lines, and the central maximum (n = 0) is the zero order. In white light each order is a continuous spectrum; for a given n, long wavelengths (red) are deviated through larger angles than short wavelengths (blue).

The sines of the deviation angles are proportional to lambda / d, so for a substantial deviation the grating spacing d should be of the same order as the wavelength. Gratings for visible light (lambda from 400 to 700 nm) usually have about 1000 slits per millimetre; d is the reciprocal of the number of slits per unit length, so d is about 1000 nm.

blocks.alt: Left: parallel red rays fall on a grating whose slits are a distance d apart; purple rays leave each slit at angle theta, and dashed orange lines show that each path is longer than the next by d sin(theta). Right: a laser shines through a grating onto a screen, giving bright spots labelled n = 2, 1, 0, -1 and -2. Below: d sin(theta) = n lambda.
blocks.caption: A diffraction grating and its orders (original diagram after Figs 15.16 and 15.17).
blocks.long_description: When the extra path between neighbouring slits is a whole number of wavelengths, all the slits reinforce each other and a sharp bright line appears. With thousands of slits, even a small change of angle spoils the match, so the lines are very sharp.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The book shows photographs of the spectrum of white light from gratings of 100 slits and of 2000 slits; with more slits the spectrum is spread out more and the colours are sharper. It also shows an 'interesting application', diffraction of radio waves around a hill, which lets radio signals reach places behind hills.

A grating has 500 lines per millimetre. Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on it normally. Find the angle of the first-order maximum. Solution: d = 1 mm / 500 = 2.0 x 10^-6 m. sin(theta) = n lambda / d = (1)(600 x 10^-9) / (2.0 x 10^-6) = 0.30, so theta = 17.5 degrees. The highest order possible is the largest n with n lambda / d below 1: n = 3 (sin(theta) = 0.90).

blocks.prompt: For a diffraction grating, what are the advantages of many slits and of closely spaced slits?
blocks.explanation: Many slits make the maxima much sharper and brighter, so wavelengths can be measured precisely and close wavelengths separated. Closely spaced slits (small d) spread the orders through larger angles, giving greater dispersion.

blocks.prompt: How would the pattern change if red light were replaced by blue light in a given grating?
blocks.explanation: Blue light has a shorter wavelength, so sin(theta) = n lambda / d is smaller for each order: the lines move closer to the central maximum, and more orders become possible.

items: Diffraction: bending into the geometrical shadow.
Grating: many equally spaced slits; d sin(theta) = n lambda.
Orders n = 0, +/-1, +/-2; red deviates more than blue; d about 1000 nm for visible light.
